claims.proposition: A long survey line across the ocean floor gives the complete sequence of reversals in one measurement.
A magnetic anomaly is the difference between the field measured at a site and the field a dipole would produce there.
A magnetometer measures the intensity of the magnetic field at the Earth's surface.
A magnetometer of the type used on research vessels can detect a field change of a few nanoTesla.
A marine magnetic anomaly survey measures the magnetic field along a ship track across the ocean floor.
A survey of the anomalies of the Pacific basin requires a track of several thousand kilometres of ship time.
Paleomagnetic measurements of cooling lava reveal the direction of the field at the time the lava hardened.
Reversals of the Earth's magnetic field have occurred at irregular intervals over the past two hundred million years.
Shipboard surveys of magnetic anomalies provided the first continuous profile of the ocean floor.
Symmetric bands of matching polarity on both flanks of a ridge provide the central evidence for seafloor spreading.
The anomaly measured over a reversing segment has the opposite sign to the field over the segment beside it.
The contribution of a single reversal to the width of the anomaly band is a function of the spreading rate and the duration of the interval.
The older anomalies occur farther from the ridge axis.
The pattern of alternating polarity in the ocean floor is a record of the reversals of the Earth's magnetic field.
The polarity sequence of the anomalies forms a mirror image on the two sides of a mid-ocean ridge.
The spacing of the anomaly bands supports a rate of seafloor spreading of a few centimetres per year.
The width of a band of matching polarity increases with the age of the crust it was created in.
The youngest anomalies occur close to the ridge axis.
A change of the rate produces a bend in the age distance relation of the survey.
A measurement of the age of crust at two distances from the axis determines the average spreading rate.
A ridge that spreads slowly produces narrow bands of crust for the same age.
An isochron map shows crust of the same age in bands that run parallel to the ridge axis.
Calculations of the age distance relation depend on a constant rate of plate motion over the measured interval.
Faster spreading produces a wider band of crust for the same age of the ocean floor.
Half rates of spreading move the crust away from the axis twice as slowly as full rates.
The age of the ocean floor increases with the distance from the ridge axis.
The distance age relation is a straight line when the spreading rate is constant.
The measurement of a spreading rate needs the age of the crust at two points on the floor.
The oldest crust in the ocean basin forms far from the ridge, and the youngest crust forms at the ridge.
The oldest measurable crust of the ocean floor is a little older than two hundred million years.
The rate of seafloor spreading changes from one ocean basin to another.
The rate of seafloor spreading controls how quickly a new band of crust forms at the ridge axis.
The rate of spreading at a ridge can change during the lifetime of a survey line.
The two points of the measurement are usually far apart, because the difference between them must be larger than the error of the age determination.
The width of a band of crust of a given age is a measure of the rate of spreading during that interval.
The youngest crust at the ridge axis is a few hundred thousand years old.
A deep ocean trench forms where one plate moves beneath another plate.
A subduction zone produces earthquakes that follow the dipping plane of the descending slab.
A subduction zone without a trench can form where the older plate is unusually dense.
Serpentinite mud volcanoes form in the forearc of a subduction zone.
The deepest earthquakes of the Wadati Benioff zone occur at depths of several hundred kilometres.
The heat of the descending slab causes partial melting of the mantle wedge above it.
The rate of convergence of the two plates determines how much sediment the forearc basin can hold.
The sediment of the forearc basin contains the material that the trench has scraped from the ocean floor.
The trench axis is the surface expression of the boundary between the two plates.
The volume of crust consumed at a subduction zone equals the volume of crust produced at a ridge.
Water depth increases sharply across a trench axis.
A hydrothermal vent releases hot mineral rich water onto the ocean floor.
Chemosynthetic bacteria use the hydrogen sulphide of the vent fluid to produce organic matter.
Chimney structures of sulphide minerals grow above a vent over years.
The animals of a vent community include tube worms and pale crabs.
The bacteria of the tube worm provide the organic matter that the worm uses.
The biological community around a vent depends on the chemosynthetic food chain rather than on sunlight.
The dissolved metals of the vent fluid are an important source for the ocean water.
The dissolved sulphide content of the fluid supports the growth of the vent community.
The first confirmed vent field was found on the floor of the Atlantic ocean.
The plume of a vent field can be followed for hundreds of metres above the floor.
The temperature of the vent fluid is high enough to melt lead.
The tube worm of a vent community has no mouth and no gut of its own.
